h1: The 6 Best Printers for Home Offices, from Laser to Inkjet, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Printers for Home Offices: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 6 home office printers from Brother, HP and Canon compared on duty cycle, document feeders, duplex printing and running costs.
summary: The Brother DCP-L2640DW is the home office printer to buy if you print a lot of text documents, with a monochrome laser engine, duplex printing and the highest duty cycle in this ranking. The HP OfficeJet Pro 8125e is the best color all-in-one with an automatic document feeder,, and the Canon PIXMA TR4720 is the budget pick that includes fax.
intro: The sticker price of a printer is the smallest part of owning one. A cheap inkjet that sips ink on every page can cost several times its purchase price in cartridges over a few years, while a laser that costs more upfront often prints thousands of pages on a single toner. Before you compare features, decide how many pages you print a month and what kind of pages they are.

We reviewed eight listings, set aside a label maker that does not replace a document printer, and ranked the seven printers that remain. The ranking uses spec sheets and listings: print technology, duplex, document feeder, duty cycle and connectivity. Cartridge prices change often, so we describe cost structure and avoid quoting numbers. Price buckets replace exact prices.

products.name: Brother DCP-L2640DW Wireless Compact Monochrome Laser Printer
products.verdict: A compact monochrome laser with duplex printing, wireless and mobile printing and the highest duty cycle here.
products.description:
The DCP-L2640DW is a compact monochrome laser all-in-one with duplex printing, wireless and mobile printing, Alexa support and the highest duty cycle ceiling in this ranking. It falls in the $200 to $500 range.

Laser is the right engine for text. Toner does not dry out the way ink does, pages come out sharp, smudge-resistant and fast, and a home office that prints contracts, invoices and reports will find the cost per page far lower than inkjet. The duty cycle, the maximum monthly pages the printer is designed for, tells you it will not struggle with sustained volume. The limit is color: you get black and white only, so colored charts and photos are out.

Buy it if text documents fill most of your printing. Skip it if you print color graphics regularly.
pros: Laser toner does not dry out
Highest duty cycle in this ranking
cons: Highest price bracket in the group
products.idealFor: Home offices that print lots of text documents.
products.skipIf: You need color charts or photos.

products.name: HP OfficeJet Pro 8125e Wireless All-in-One Color Inkjet Printer
products.verdict: A color inkjet with an automatic document feeder, duplex printing and a 3-month Instant Ink trial.
products.description:
The OfficeJet Pro 8125e is a wireless color all-in-one with an automatic document feeder, duplex printing, a 3-month Instant Ink trial and AI-enabled setup. It is rated for home office use and priced in the $50 to $100 bracket.

The document feeder is the feature that justifies the rank. Scanning or copying a multi-page contract by hand, one sheet at a time, wastes a surprising amount of time. Duplex printing halves paper use. Color is there when you need it for a presentation. The trial of Instant Ink, HP's ink subscription, is useful for the first months but is not the whole story: after it ends, you either subscribe, with the conditions that come with it, or buy cartridges.

Buy it if you scan and copy regularly and want color. Skip it if you want to avoid subscription services.
cons: Inkjet cartridges cost more per page
products.idealFor: Offices that scan, copy and print in color.
products.skipIf: You want to avoid ink subscriptions.

products.name: HP OfficeJet Pro 8125 Wireless All-in-One Color Inkjet Printer
products.verdict: The same OfficeJet family with a feeder, duplex and a 3-month Instant Ink trial, for two or three people on one network.
products.description:
The 8125 shares the 8125e's specs: wireless color all-in-one, automatic document feeder, duplex printing, a 3-month Instant Ink trial and AI-capable setup. It is rated for home office use and sits in the $100 to $200 bracket.

It places behind the e model purely on listing detail and positioning. Both are aimed at households where two or three people print from different devices over wifi, and both benefit from a feeder. The listing here is a little less clear on its edition and costs more according to its bracket, so the e version is the safer buy. If the two cost the same on the day, the specs are close enough that either one will serve.

Buy it if it is cheaper than the e model on the day or if it is the one in stock. Check the model number printed on the listing before you pay.
cons: Costs more than the e model
products.idealFor: Two or three people printing over wifi.

products.name: Canon PIXMA TR4720 All-in-One Wireless Printer
products.verdict: A budget wireless all-in-one with an automatic document feeder, built-in fax and mobile printing.
products.description:
The PIXMA TR4720 is a wireless all-in-one with an automatic document feeder, a built-in fax, mobile printing support and the lowest price in this list. It sits in the $50 to $100 bracket.

The fax matters more than people expect: some businesses, doctors and landlords still insist on it, and a printer with built-in fax means no separate machine. With a feeder, it handles multi-page scans too. It ranks fourth because it is a standard cartridge inkjet with higher per-page costs than a laser, and because the listing gives no duplex support, which the HP and Brother offer.

Buy it if you are a single-user office on a tight budget that needs to fax or scan stacks. Skip it if you print a lot, where ink costs will add up.
cons: Ink costs rise with heavy use
products.idealFor: Single-user offices that still need fax.
products.skipIf: You print hundreds of pages a month.

products.name: Canon PIXMA TS6520 Wireless Color Inkjet Printer
products.verdict: A compact color inkjet with duplex printing, a 1.42 inch OLED display and a simple control panel.
products.description:
The TS6520 is a compact wireless color inkjet with duplex printing, a 1.42 inch OLED display and an intuitive control panel. It falls in the $50 to $100 bracket.

The OLED display is a small but real convenience, since it shows status and errors without a trip to your computer. It is built for a home office shared by two or three people on the same wifi network. It ranks fifth because the listing shows no document feeder, and for a business user who scans paperwork that is the feature that saves time. Without it, you scan by hand.

Buy it if you share the printer and want duplex and a simple panel. Skip it if you need to copy or scan multi-page documents.
products.idealFor: Shared wifi offices with light scanning.

products.name: Canon PIXMA TS4320 Wireless Color Inkjet Printer
products.verdict: A compact wireless inkjet with duplex printing, a 1-year limited warranty and easy setup.
products.description:
The TS4320 is a compact color inkjet with duplex printing, a built-in copier and scanner, a 1-year limited warranty and easy setup. It falls in the $50 to $100 bracket.

It earns its place because it fits in tight corners and the warranty is clearly stated. Duplex is welcome at this price. It ranks sixth because it is the basic end of the Canon range: no feeder, no display, and a small footprint comes at the cost of paper capacity. For a corner desk in a small room it is a sensible fit, and setup is simple.

Buy it if space is the main constraint. Skip it if you print or scan in volume.
products.skipIf: You scan or print in volume.

methodology.title: Print technology and cost structure
methodology.description: We compared monochrome laser with color inkjet, since toner and ink behave differently when a printer sits idle between jobs.

methodology.title: Document handling
methodology.description: Automatic document feeders and duplex printing were weighed for how much time and paper they save an office user.

methodology.title: Duty cycle and volume
methodology.description: Duty cycle ceilings and the sizes of each printer's intended household or office were checked against likely monthly volume.

methodology.title: Connectivity and sharing
methodology.description: Wireless, mobile printing and shared use over one network were compared for two- and three-person offices.

methodology.title: Subscription and warranty
methodology.description: Instant Ink trials and stated warranties were noted, since ink plans change the long-term cost of a printer.

whatMatters.detail: Laser printers use toner that does not dry out, print text fast and cost less per page at volume. Inkjets print color and photos well but use cartridges that clog if unused. Choose by what you print most, not by the cheapest sticker.

A feeder lets you scan or copy a stack without lifting the lid for each page. It is a major time saver for contracts and receipts. Look for ADF or automatic document feeder on the listing, as on the HP OfficeJet and Canon TR4720.
Automatic two-sided printing cuts paper use in half and makes documents look tidy. Many cheap printers print duplex only by hand. Check for the word automatic before you assume the feature.

The duty cycle is the maximum pages a printer is designed to handle per month. Running far below it is normal, and running above it shortens life. The Brother laser has the highest ceiling here, which suits sustained use.

HP's Instant Ink and similar plans can lower the cost per page, but they tie the printer to a service and may stop working if you cancel. Read the terms before you enroll. A plan trial is not the same as a permanent price.

cards.text: A document feeder for scanning forms, duplex printing for contracts, wireless setup and a reliable text engine. Fax is still needed by some employers.

cards.text: The Brother DCP-L2640DW for text, the HP OfficeJet Pro 8125e for scanning, and the Canon TR4720 for fax.

faq.q: Do these printers work with Mac and Windows?
faq.a: Yes, all of them print wirelessly from both, and most support mobile printing. Check the maker's driver page for your operating system version before you buy.

faq.q: What is the biggest mistake when buying an office printer?
faq.a: Choosing on purchase price alone. A cheap inkjet used heavily can cost more in cartridges than a laser costs to buy. Estimate your monthly pages first and compare cost per page.

faq.q: Is the Brother laser worth it over an HP OfficeJet?
faq.a: If you print mostly text, yes. The toner lasts longer and costs less per page. If you need color, an automatic feeder for color scans or photos, the HP OfficeJet is the better fit.
Most are ready in 10 to 20 minutes: unpack, install the ink or toner, load paper, connect to wifi from the app and test a page. HP and Canon apps guide the process.

faq.q: How do I stop ink from drying out?
faq.a: Print a page or two each week and leave the printer on standby. Cartridges that sit idle clog, especially in dry climates. A laser avoids this problem entirely.

faq.q: Do I need an Instant Ink subscription?
faq.a: No. The trials on the HP models are optional, and you can buy cartridges instead. A subscription can save money at certain volumes, but read the terms, since the plan can lock the printer to the service.

finalTake: For text-heavy home offices, the Brother DCP-L2640DW is the best printer here, with a laser engine, duplex and the highest duty cycle. Color users should choose the HP OfficeJet Pro 8125e for its feeder, and the Canon PIXMA TR4720 is the budget answer if you still fax. Estimate your monthly pages before you compare prices, because running cost beats sticker price.
